task.goal: Make a 20-square-meter room support both remote work and exercise without buying major furniture.
hard_constraints: One person has a foldable desk, mat and limited storage; no drilling or electrical rewiring.
Keep a clear exit path and avoid daily setup taking more than ten minutes.
Compare usable floor area, switching effort and clutter over one week.
task.available_resources: Existing shelves, boxes and a tape measure.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Permanent work and exercise zones
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: give each activity a permanent footprint, eliminating furniture movement. Place the unfolded desk against a suitable wall and reserve a separate exercise rectangle, with the exit route outside both zones. What changes the outcome is whether both footprints fit simultaneously; the room’s stated 20 square meters alone does not establish this.

Measure the room, door swing, shelves, desk and mat. Include chair pullback and the space needed for the actual exercises, rather than counting only the mat. Use the existing outlet location when choosing the work corner so cables do not cross circulation space. Put work supplies on one existing shelf and exercise supplies in one box. Keep the mat down only if it lies flat and creates no trip hazard; otherwise roll it beside its zone. Move boxes into existing storage without unstable stacking or obstructing access.

This needs no purchases, drilling or rewiring. It assumes the remaining furniture leaves two useful areas and a clear route to the door. Its strengths are low switching effort and stable boundaries for clutter. Its limit is a smaller maximum exercise area: this may suit stretching and stationary workouts but fail for movements requiring travel.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare with the current arrangement over seven days: record two baseline days, then five zoned days with comparable work and exercise sessions. Each day measure the largest clear exercise rectangle and usable work footprint, time all setup and pack-away, and count items left outside their assigned storage. Record any exit obstruction separately. Inspect door opening and chair pullback before use. Reject this layout if either activity cannot fit safely, the exit route is compromised, or daily setup exceeds ten minutes. A smaller exercise area is acceptable only if it supports the intended routine; no improvement is assumed before measurement.

DIRECT_FULL.title: One shared floor area with a folded desk
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: reuse the same central footprint at different times. The foldable desk occupies it during work and moves into a defined storage position for exercise. Unlike permanent zoning, this exchanges switching effort for a larger uninterrupted exercise area.

Measure a clear exercise rectangle and identify a nearby desk parking position that leaves the door, exit route and shelves accessible. Check the desk’s folding instructions and stability; store it only in a position where it cannot fall or slide. Assign one existing box to loose work items and a shelf position to that box. At the end of work, pack the box, disconnect and stow cables, fold and park the desk, move any chair into its measured parking footprint, then unroll the mat. Reverse the sequence for work. Keep frequently needed items together so clearing the desk does not become individual-item sorting.

The necessary assumptions are that one person can safely fold and move the desk, suitable parking exists, and the work equipment can tolerate daily packing. No new furniture or building changes are needed. This approach offers the greatest potential shared floor area, but the parked desk and chair still consume space. Heavy equipment, a fragile monitor or an awkward folding mechanism could make it impractical.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: During one week, use the current desk-open arrangement for two baseline days and the shared-footprint arrangement for five days. Measure the largest clear exercise rectangle in each state, time both switching directions, and count loose items remaining after pack-away. Count the combined daily setup and reset time against a ten-minute ceiling. First perform one complete dry run without exercising: reject the design immediately if parking is unstable, lifting is unsafe or the exit route narrows. Reject it after the week if the extra usable exercise area is negligible or the repeated handling exceeds the time budget.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Keep the desk fixed; change the exercise footprint
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: adapt the workout to the room’s existing clear spaces instead of making the room accommodate a large exercise zone. Keep the desk open in its normal work position and use a compact mat station for floor exercises plus an adjacent standing station used sequentially. This changes the space requirement of the activity itself.

Measure the available mat footprint and standing clearance, including overhead reach and distance from shelves, desk corners and the door swing. Choose a routine that achieves the person’s intended training purpose within these bounds—for example, controlled squats, stationary lunges and mat-based strength or mobility movements, where suitable for their ability. Exclude movements needing travel, jumping clearance or furniture support unless their safety is established. Reorient the mat between exercise blocks only if necessary; do not reposition it between every movement. Store it rolled with any exercise items in one accessible box or shelf space. Leave work equipment in place and keep cables contained outside both exercise stations and the exit route.

This requires only measuring, routine selection and a small storage assignment. It assumes the exercise goal can be served by stationary movements. It offers minimal furniture handling and less work-item clutter, but does not create more floor area or preserve every preferred workout. Suitability for the person’s fitness needs remains uncertain.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Over seven days, compare two days using the usual arrangement and routine with five days using the compact routine. Record the measured clear exercise footprint, switching time, misplaced-item count and whether the intended session was completed without constrained movements. Include one slow rehearsal of every movement to check limb clearance before normal exercise. Keep the same intended training purpose when comparing sessions. Reject this option if it sacrifices essential exercises, causes contact with furnishings, compromises the exit route or requires more than ten minutes of daily setup. Its success depends on adequate exercise within less space, not an assumed increase in usable area.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Reclaim floor space by consolidating storage
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: reduce the footprint of stored belongings so work and exercise can coexist without moving the desk each day. The outcome changes only if existing floor storage can be absorbed into safely available shelf capacity. This creates usable space by compressing storage, rather than alternating furniture positions or changing the workout.

Measure the floor footprints of boxes and other stored items, then inspect the existing shelves for unused capacity and loosely packed contents. Group compatible belongings into fewer existing boxes, nest empty boxes, and transfer suitable contents to accessible shelf spaces. Keep heavy items low, respect known shelf load limits, and avoid tall stacks or loading freestanding shelves in ways that make them unstable. Do not count space as reclaimed if displaced belongings obstruct another part of the room.

Use the recovered floor area for the mat and the clearance required by the intended exercises. Keep the desk open, with chair pullback and cables outside that clearance. Preserve the door swing and a continuous exit path in both activity states. Give frequently used work items one accessible shelf location so they do not gradually occupy the recovered area. Daily switching should require only parking the chair safely and rolling or unrolling the mat.

Implementation needs only the tape measure, existing shelves and boxes, plus a one-time sorting session. It assumes some floor storage is compressible and the shelves have suitable spare capacity. It fails where storage is already efficient, shelves are unsuitable, or the recovered patch is too narrow for the actual exercises. The room’s total area does not establish feasibility.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment:
Compare two baseline days with five days after consolidation. In each arrangement, measure the largest unobstructed exercise rectangle and usable desk-and-chair footprint; do not count disconnected gaps as exercise area. Record total daily setup and reset minutes and count items left outside assigned storage at the same time each evening. Record the one-time sorting effort separately.

Before moving everything, trial consolidation with one floor box and inspect whether its complete footprint becomes usable without blocking shelf access or the exit. After rearranging, rehearse the intended exercises slowly. Reject the design if storage becomes unstable, either activity lacks clearance, the exit is obstructed, or daily switching exceeds ten minutes. If clutter repeatedly returns to the recovered floor space during the week, the storage arrangement has not demonstrated a sustainable benefit.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Use a suitable existing shelf as the work surface
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: give an existing shelf a second function as the workstation, allowing the foldable desk to remain safely stored throughout the week. This removes the desk’s deployed footprint without daily folding or moving work equipment. What changes the outcome is whether the shelving can actually support comfortable, stable work while leaving a useful exercise area.

First inspect an accessible shelf for sufficient depth, suitable working height, legroom and capacity for the actual work equipment. Reuse an existing chair if seated work fits; consider standing work only if comfortable for the intended work periods. Do not remove structural shelf members, improvise a cantilevered surface, or use a unit that requires additional anchoring. If suitable stability or load capacity cannot be established, reject this option.

Move the shelf’s displaced contents into existing boxes or spare shelf space, counting their new footprint. Trial the workstation before storing the desk. Keep cables close to the shelving using the existing outlet arrangement. Store the folded desk in a stable position outside the door swing and exit route. Measure the resulting exercise rectangle, including movement clearance beyond the mat. Daily switching consists of leaving the workstation, positioning the mat and returning it to storage.

This needs only existing shelving, boxes, the desk and a tape measure. It assumes a shelf suitable for sustained work already exists and that displaced belongings can be accommodated. Many shelves will fail the ergonomic or stability requirements; suitability is unknown. Its potential benefit is eliminating a separate work surface from the floor plan, but awkward posture or reduced storage could outweigh that gain.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment:
Use the normal desk for two baseline days and the shelf workstation for five days. Before committing, complete a representative work session and slowly rehearse the intended exercises. Reject the trial for discomfort, shelf movement, inadequate equipment support or restricted exercise clearance.

For both arrangements, measure usable work clearance and the largest clear exercise rectangle; record total daily switching time and count belongings outside assigned storage each evening. Include the stored desk and displaced shelf contents when assessing floor use and clutter. Inspect the exit route in both activity states. Reject the design if the route is obstructed, daily setup and reset exceed ten minutes, or the shelf arrangement provides no useful floor-area gain while worsening comfort or clutter.

EXPAND.title: Recover floor space by consolidating storage
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: reduce the floor area occupied by stored belongings so work and exercise can coexist with little daily switching. The decisive change is moving floor-stored contents into existing shelf capacity and nesting empty boxes, rather than assigning activity zones or repeatedly folding the desk. This works only if dispersed storage currently consumes useful floor space and the shelves have spare, suitable capacity.

Measure the room, door swing, desk with chair pulled back, and floor occupied by boxes or loose belongings. Inspect shelf stability and loading limits. Group belongings by frequency of use: keep daily work supplies within easy reach, put occasional-use contents into existing boxes on suitable shelves, and nest unused boxes. Keep heavy contents low, avoid projecting boxes or unstable stacks, and leave frequently used items accessible without unpacking other containers. Do not use boxes as improvised furniture or increase shelf loading beyond what can be established as safe.

Use the recovered space for the intended exercise movements, checking limb clearance beyond the mat. Keep the desk available for work and return the rolled mat to an accessible storage position afterward. Route existing cables outside the exercise space and exit path.

Implementation needs only the tape measure, existing shelves and boxes, plus a one-time sorting session. The daily benefit comes from reducing the number of objects occupying the floor. Its limits are available shelf capacity and the amount of recoverable space; a room already free of floor storage gains little. Putting everyday items into inconvenient storage could also replace visible clutter with repeated rummaging.
EXPAND.experiment: Compare two days of the existing arrangement with five days after consolidation. In both conditions, record the largest unobstructed exercise rectangle, usable work footprint including chair clearance, total daily setup and reset minutes, and number of items left outside assigned storage. Record exit obstructions separately. Before reorganizing everything, consolidate one representative group of floor-stored items and measure whether its removal creates contiguous, useful clearance. Reject the approach if safe shelving capacity is insufficient, the recovered space cannot support the intended workout, daily handling exceeds ten minutes, or clutter repeatedly returns to the floor. This comparison is exploratory; changes in belongings or activity across the week could affect the result.

EXPAND.title: Use an existing shelf as the work surface
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: replace the desk’s working footprint with a suitable surface on an existing shelving unit, then keep the foldable desk safely stored for the week. This changes which furniture supports work, potentially releasing floor space without daily desk handling. Unlike moving belongings onto shelves, it depends on transferring the work activity itself.

First inspect whether any shelf can support the actual work equipment safely and comfortably. It needs adequate depth, an appropriate working height, usable legroom for seated work or comfortable reach for standing work, and sufficient stability without new wall fixings. Do not remove structural shelves, extend a surface with boxes, or use a unit that rocks or requires anchoring. If these conditions cannot be met, reject this alternative.

Measure the shelf workstation, the stored desk footprint, and the clearance needed for the intended exercises. Locate equipment near an existing outlet, with cables outside the movement area and exit route. Relocate displaced shelf contents only into available boxes or shelf space; the design fails if this merely transfers clutter onto the floor. Store the folded desk where it cannot tip, slide, or obstruct access. Keep the mat accessible for a short daily rollout and return.

Implementation requires the tape measure, existing storage, and a one-time rearrangement. It assumes the work equipment fits and the shelf permits a sustainable posture. Standing-only work may be unsuitable for a full workday; brief standing breaks do not correct a poorly fitted workstation. The potential benefit is a larger exercise area with little switching effort, but shelf dimensions, safe loading and comfort remain unverified.
EXPAND.experiment: Over seven days, use the original desk arrangement on days 1–2 and the shelf arrangement on days 3–7, provided the initial safety inspection passes. Record the largest clear exercise rectangle, total daily switching minutes, and the number of loose objects left outside assigned storage each evening. Check the exit route in both modes. Start with a short real work session; stop if posture, reach or stability is unacceptable. Reject the design if it gains no usable area, displaces clutter onto the floor, impairs work, or exceeds ten minutes of daily setup. This is a practical comparison, not proof of long-term comfort.
